title: Samosa Chaat Brings Tangy, Sweet Crunch to Diwali House Party Menus
excerpt: Crisp samosas layered with chole, two chutneys, spiced yogurt and sev — components ahead, assembly at the last moment
body:
• Samosa chaat turns crisp samosas into a layered party snack with chole, chutneys, spiced yogurt, onion, cilantro and sev.
  • For a Diwali house party, make the components ahead and assemble only when serving, so the samosa pieces stay crisp under the toppings.
  • The recipe card below serves 4, with 10 minutes of preparation and 15 minutes of cooking, not counting the chole.
  • Balance is the technique: sweet tamarind chutney against spicy cilantro chutney, and cool raita against warm, spiced chickpeas.

A Diwali house party needs at least one snack that guests can eat standing up, return to for seconds, and talk about between courses. Samosa chaat fits that brief because it is built, not cooked to order: crisp samosas are lightly smashed and broken, then layered with chole, chutneys, spiced yogurt and crunchy toppings. The result is sweet, spicy, tangy and crisp in the same bite, and it can be served in wide bowls or small individual portions for a party table.

The idea, promoted this Diwali as a homemade house-party recipe, is not new. Samosa chaat is a well-established Indian street-food dish in which a plain samosa becomes the base for a full plate of toppings. One detailed recipe describes samosas served with chole — chana masala — and a sweet, spicy, tangy and crispy array of toppings. Another describes the same structure from the street-food side: crispy samosas topped with chickpeas, chutneys, yogurt and crunchy sev. The agreement between those recipes is the method a home cook can rely on.

Build the components first

Start with the samosas. Homemade samosas are a project, so for a party it is reasonable to use good store-bought samosas and crisp them before serving. The chole should be made in quantity: it is a chickpea dish made by cooking chickpeas and simmering them with aromatics, tomatoes and spices, and extra chole can be used later in rolls, rice bowls or another meal. Make more than the chaat requires rather than trying to calculate the exact amount on the night.

Prepare the two chutneys next. The cilantro chutney in the recipe card is processed from fresh cilantro, green chili, ginger, lime juice, ground cumin, amchur powder, water and salt. The tamarind chutney provides the sweet contrast; it can be homemade or bought. Finally, stir together the raita — in this recipe a vegan version made with plant-based yogurt, lime juice, ground cumin, amchur powder, salt and chopped cilantro. Whisked yogurt is what cools the plate and balances the chili heat.

"Samosa chaat is a well-established Indian street-food dish in which a plain samosa becomes the base for a full plate of toppings."

Assemble at the last moment

Assembly is the part that decides whether the dish works. To assemble one serving, add half a cup to one cup of chole to a wide bowl, lightly smash the samosas and break up the pieces, and top with a little more chole. Then drizzle on the cilantro chutney, tamarind chutney and raita, and finish with chopped red onion, cilantro and sev.

Do not assemble the whole batch in advance. Recipes for the dish are consistent on this point: prep the chutneys, yogurt and chickpeas ahead, but assemble only when ready to serve, and eat immediately while the samosas are still crisp. For a house party, that suggests a practical setup — bowls of warm chole, broken samosa pieces, both chutneys, raita, onion, cilantro and sev laid out in order, with the host assembling each bowl to order or guests building their own. That keeps the line moving and prevents a tray of chaat from going soggy while guests are still arriving.

How to serve it at a Diwali party

Serve the chaat in small bowls rather than on flat plates, so the chole and chutneys stay with the samosa pieces. Keep extra sev and chopped onion on the table for guests who want more crunch, and keep the green chili level adjustable through the chutney rather than seasoning the whole batch hot. A pinch of chaat masala is listed as optional in the recipe, and it is best added at the end, to taste.

The recipe card gives the full quantities as published in the source recipe: eight samosas, one recipe of chole, half a red onion and half a cup of cilantro for the chaat itself, plus the separate chutney and raita components. No nutrition figures are given for that recipe, so none are claimed here. With the components ready, the active work at serving time is only a few minutes per bowl — which is exactly what a Diwali host needs when the doorbell, not the stove, is setting the pace.

steps: Process all the ingredients for the green chutney in a small food processor, adding a little water at a time until it is mostly smooth.
Stir all the ingredients for the raita in a bowl.
To assemble one serving, add 1/2 to 1 cup chole to a wide bowl.
Slightly smash the samosas and break up the pieces, and place them on the chole.
Top with a little more chole.
Drizzle on the cilantro chutney, tamarind chutney and raita.
Finish with onions, cilantro and sev, and serve immediately.
